stories.headline: Experts adopt AI agent's random opinions and think they're their own, Anthropic study finds
stories.claim: Anthropic study finds experts adopted an AI agent's randomly assigned preferences and mostly believed the conclusions were their own.
stories.summary: An Anthropic experiment with 50 causal-inference experts found that participants adopted the AI agent's assigned preference in 86 percent of four analytical decisions, far above chance. The agent had been given a coin-toss preference and only made honest arguments for its side. Most participants still felt the final recommendation was their own, and 77 percent used the agent's arguments in their explanations. The researchers warn that shared default AI preferences could create false consensus in science and weaken human checks on AI safety research. AI-assisted analyses also had far fewer serious flaws, 6 percent against 55 percent without AI.
key_points: Experts adopted the agent's randomly assigned preference in 86 percent of four analytical decisions.
Most participants believed the final recommendation was mostly or entirely their own.
77 percent used at least one of the agent's arguments in their explanations, often in nearly the same words.
AI-assisted analyses had serious flaws in 6 percent of cases, compared with 55 percent without AI.
The researchers warn of false consensus in science and risks to AI safety evaluations, and call for tools to measure deference.

The discoveries matter for drug design, since mirror-image forms of a molecule can behave very differently.

stories.headline: Traders' tools stolen every 20 minutes in UK
stories.claim: Tool thefts in the UK were recorded roughly every 20 minutes in 2025, with at least 26,164 reported across 30 forces.

stories.headline: Bank of Japan says inflation hit 2% target after 13 years
stories.claim: The Bank of Japan says underlying inflation has reached its 2% target for the first time since it was set in 2013, and kept rates at 1.25%.
stories.summary: The Bank of Japan said on Friday that underlying consumer price inflation is now at a level generally consistent with its 2% price stability target, the first time it has formally confirmed this since the goal was set in 2013. The central bank kept its key interest rate unchanged at 1.25%, with an eight-to-one vote, after the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank held rates earlier in the week. The BoJ warned that core CPI excluding fresh food is likely to accelerate to clearly above 2%, citing energy and goods prices, chip prices linked to AI demand and yen weakness. Core inflation in September was 2.1%. Analysts expect further tightening, with Capital Economics forecasting a 2% policy rate by mid-next-year, while Japanese officials are expected to hike in December.

stories.headline: Topcoat enables Rust to render server-side web apps

stories.summary: Carl Lerche, an Amazon Web Services principal engineer and creator of the Tokio runtime, presented Topcoat at ScyllaDB's 2026 P99 virtual conference. Topcoat is a framework for building web applications in Rust. It compiles Rust into JavaScript rather than WebAssembly, and most logic runs on the server, with only results sent to the browser. Lerche said it suits typical database-driven web apps rather than very complex applications. It draws on server-side rendering approaches such as HTMX, Datastar and Phoenix LiveView, and connects components directly to the database through his Toasty project. Ken Kohlman, a frontend developer, praised its simplicity while noting it only supports a subset of Rust syntax.

stories.headline: Someone ran Rivian’s pedal-by-wire e-bike out of battery and things got weird
stories.claim: A owner's test of the ALSO TM-B pedal-by-wire e-bike found it keeps limited assistance on low battery but had odd behaviour and heavy overnight drain.
stories.summary: An early Launch Edition owner, Aaron Draczynski, ran the ALSO TM-B e-bike down to empty to test its pedal-by-wire system and shared the results on YouTube. As the battery fell, the bike progressively cut its maximum assist, down to Level 1, before electric assistance stopped at 4% charge. The bike then entered what the owner called Infinite Turtle Mode, where pedalling energy is passed through the electronic drivetrain. He said it was workable on flat ground but very hard on hills, with manual shifting disabled. Separately, the bike drained from 70% to 18% over about two days while parked, and then showed a battery error that a physical reset button fixed. The owner suspects the lack of a cell signal may be the cause.
key_points: The ALSO TM-B has no mechanical link between pedals and rear wheel; both are electronically connected.

stories.headline: General Motors agrees to pay $220 million to settle multi-state data privacy lawsuit
stories.claim: General Motors agrees to pay $220 million to settle a multi-state lawsuit over selling driver data without consent.
stories.summary: General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle a lawsuit brought by the attorneys general of 35 US states and the District of Columbia. The case concerns the company's OnStar Smart Driver programme, through which GM allegedly collected driving data from 2016 to 2024 and sold it to data brokers, which insurers used to raise premiums. The AGs said more than 370,000 drivers were wrongly told they were not enrolled, and their data was still sold. Under the settlement, GM must limit the driving data it collects and protect personal information, and it faces mandated privacy assessments and staff training. The settlement follows a Federal Trade Commission ban earlier this year on sharing certain consumer data for five years, and a $12.75 million settlement with California in May.

stories.headline: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
stories.claim: Companies are increasingly using AI agents as co-workers, creating productivity gains but also job losses and workplace tension.
stories.summary: A Guardian feature looks at how US startups and corporations are adopting AI agents as co-workers, handling tasks such as scheduling, coding, marketing and customer onboarding. AI startup Anything has around 15 human staff and roughly 150 agents, and its founder expects AI co-workers to outnumber humans at most companies within a year. Lindy cut about a third of its staff and filled roles with agents, while a Los Angeles production company now runs largely on agents. McKinsey reports about 40% of large organisations used AI agents between May 2025 and June 2026, up from 27% a year earlier. The article also notes tension, including customer alienation, job losses and employees becoming managers of error-prone bots.

stories.headline: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
stories.claim: China expelled a record 33 members from the Communist Party at the fifth plenum amid Xi's purges.
stories.summary: China expelled a record 33 members from the Chinese Communist Party at the fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials held roughly once a year. Only 279 of the 376 Central Committee members named in 2022 attended, the highest number of empty seats in modern Chinese history. Confirmed expulsions included former military second-in-command Zhang Youxia and former Xinjiang party secretary Ma Xingrui. The Central Military Commission now has only two members, Xi Jinping and anti-graft chief Zhang Shengmin, who was promoted to the Politburo. The plenum set up the 21st Party Congress, expected in the second half of 2027, where Xi is expected to seek a fourth term.

stories.summary: Three people died after a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter collided midair near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon on Thursday afternoon. Intel is shifting production across its fabs, including some PC chip capacity, to make more datacenter products.

The exchange later put the affected funds at about $6.3 billion, and Tether and Circle froze significant stablecoin balances to help. Binance paused deposits and withdrawals, then reopened deposits while withdrawals stayed paused for a security overhaul. It said the likely entry point was a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, and it has pledged to cover all losses from its SAFU reserve fund and company funds. The exchange says it has found no evidence of a wallet private key leak and has revoked the attacker's address authorisation.
Binance says it will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and company funds, and will publish an updated proof of reserves.
Deposits have resumed, but withdrawals remain paused for a security overhaul expected to finish within about 48 hours of the update.

stories.headline: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
stories.claim: Scientists found avian cholera, not bird flu, killed hundreds of Adélie penguins near the Antarctic Peninsula in 2024.
stories.summary: Researchers led by wildlife veterinarian Ralph Vanstreels investigated a mass die-off of Adélie penguins at the Danger Islands off the Antarctic Peninsula in March 2024. Expecting bird flu, the team found more than 537 carcasses on a single landing ramp alone, with thousands dead overall, but viral loads were low. Later lab work in the Netherlands identified a bacterial infection causing avian cholera. The findings were published in October in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The study highlights the need for broader disease surveillance, as avian cholera has rarely been tested for in the region in recent decades.
key_points: In March 2024, researchers visiting the Danger Islands off the Antarctic Peninsula found more than 537 dead Adélie penguins on one landing ramp alone.
Early tests found bird flu present but at low levels, so the team investigated further.
Later analysis identified a bacterial infection causing avian cholera, which is distinct from human cholera.
The findings were published in October in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
The researchers say the disease poses little risk to humans but can kill birds, especially in cold environments.
The last search for avian cholera in the Antarctic Peninsula was about 25 years ago, prompting calls for wider monitoring.

stories.headline: Hassett Sees Fed Inclined To Raise Rates If October Inflation Comes In Hot

stories.headline: Stranded Cambodia cruise ship ‘asked passengers for fuel money’ as crew members still not paid
stories.claim: Stranded US cruise ship MV Odyssey in Cambodia has residents out of pocket as operator Villa Vie cites fuel costs and losses.
stories.summary: The MV Odyssey, a residential world cruise ship operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, is stranded in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, after running out of fuel. Guests were told on Monday they had to disembark that day, and residents say they were repeatedly asked for extra money for fuel and that crew have not been paid. The operator says fuel costs per cabin have risen from about $1,800 to $6,000–$8,000 a month in parts of Asia because of the war in Iran and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Villa Vie said it could no longer carry the operating losses, and the ship has no departure date. Former and current residents describe lost savings and poor communication.

stories.headline: More than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a result
stories.claim: A Victorian survey finds 55% of lawyers now use AI, but only about a quarter have cut client fees as a result.
stories.summary: A 2026 census of 2,221 Victorian lawyers, run by the Victorian Legal Services Board and a legal services research centre, found AI use rose from 37% to 55% in the past year. Trade practices, banking and finance, and IT and telecoms lawyers were the heaviest users, while criminal and family law used it less. Most lawyers rely on consumer chatbots such as ChatGPT, with only 22% using legal-specific tools. Just 26% said AI had lowered client fees, and nearly half reported extra work from clients arriving with inaccurate AI-generated information. The findings suggest efficiency gains have been smaller than expected.

stories.claim: Versace confirms Pieter Mulier's debut Atelier Versace couture show at Paris Couture Week in January.

stories.claim: Human Made has opened a three-floor flagship in Harajuku, Tokyo, with a digital-physical shopping concept.
stories.summary: Streetwear brand Human Made has opened its first proper flagship store in Harajuku, Tokyo, spread over three floors. The space, designed by the studio I IN, is four times the size of its previous stores and stocks the full range, including its first original sneaker, the Duck Kick. Customers can scan product QR codes with their phones to order, with staff fetching items from storage in real time.

stories.headline: The Most Consequential Ballot Measures for the 2026 Midterm Elections
stories.claim: Voters in the 3 November 2026 US midterms will decide nearly 150 statewide ballot measures on tax, abortion, trans rights and voter ID.
stories.summary: Harper's Bazaar has published a guide to the most significant US statewide ballot measures ahead of the 3 November 2026 midterm elections, with nearly 150 measures to be decided. The highlights include California's Proposition 40, a one-time 5 percent tax on net worth above $1 billion, which Governor Gavin Newsom opposes. Rival measures 41 and 42 would undermine it, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly backed them. Abortion-rights measures are on ballots in Idaho, Virginia, Nevada and Missouri, and several states are voting on trans athletes and voter ID rules.
key_points: Nearly 150 statewide measures will be decided on 3 November 2026.
California's Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on net worth above $1 billion, estimated to raise about $100 billion over five years.
Propositions 41 and 42 are rival measures that could invalidate Proposition 40 if passed.
Abortion-rights measures appear in Idaho, Virginia, Nevada and Missouri.
Several states will vote on trans athlete rules and on voter ID requirements.
stories.market_take: A California billionaire tax would be a notable fiscal and investor-sentiment issue if passed, though the effect on markets is uncertain.
